question.text: A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $y=-3.$ Given that the point $P(1,-3,8)$ lies on $C$, and that $f_x = \dfrac{x^2+1}{x^2y^2} + y\sqrt{x}$, find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$
question.explanation:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=-3.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P(1,-3,8)$ will be given by the partial derivative $f_x(1,-3).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $f_x(x,y)$ at $(1,-3)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_x(1,-3) &= \dfrac{1^2+1}{1^2(-3)^2} + (-3)\sqrt{1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{9} - 3(1) \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{25}{9} \end{align*}

question.text: A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $x=2.$ Given that the point $P$ with $y$-coordinate $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ lies on $C$, and that $f_y = {y} \sin{\left(x y - \dfrac{\pi}{3} \right)}$, find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$
question.explanation:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point where $y=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ will be given by the partial derivative $f_y\left(2,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $f_y(x,y)$ at $\left(2,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_y\left(2,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) &= \dfrac{\pi}{4} \cdot \sin{\left(2\cdot \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{\pi}{3} \right)}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\pi}{4} \sin{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6} \right)} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\pi}{4}\cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\pi}{8} \end{align*}

question.explanation:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point where $y=0$ will be given by the partial derivative $f_y\left(1,0\right).$

question.text: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=2.$ Given that the point $P\left(2,\dfrac{\pi}{4},0\right)$ lies on $C$, and that $f_y = 4 \sin(x y)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.explanation:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z = f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P\left(2,\dfrac{\pi}{4},0\right)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial y} \Bigg|_{(2,\pi/4)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial y}$ at $\left(2,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_y\left(2,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) &= 4 \cdot \sin{\left(2 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{4} \right)} \\[5pt] &=4 \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \\[5pt] &= 4 \cdot 1 \\[5pt] &= 4 \end{align*}

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

\begin{align*} z - z|_{(2,\pi/4)} &= \dfrac {\partial z} {\partial y}\Bigg |_{(2,\pi/4)}\left(y-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \\[5pt] z - 0 &=4\left(y-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \\[5pt] z &= 4y - \pi \end{align*}

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P\left(2,\dfrac{\pi}{4},0\right)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x = 2 \\[5pt] z = 4y - \pi \end{cases} \]

question.text: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P\left(0,1,2\right)$ lies on $C$, and that $f_x = x^2+y^2-\ln(x+y)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.explanation:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z = f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P\left(0,1,2\right)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial x} \Bigg|_{\left(0,1\right)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial x}$ at $\left(0,1\right)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial z} {\partial x}\Bigg |_{\left(0,1\right)} &= (0)^2+(1)^2-\ln(0+1) \\[3pt] &= 1 - \ln 1 \\[3pt] &= 1- 0 \\[3pt] &= 1 \end{align*}

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

\begin{align*} z - z|_{\left(0,1\right)} &= \dfrac {\partial z} {\partial x}\Bigg |_{\left(0,1\right)}\left(x-0\right) \\[5pt] z - 2 &= 1\left(x\right) \\[5pt] z &= x + 2 \end{align*}

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P\left(0,1,2\right)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows: \[ \begin{cases} y = 1 \\ z = x+2 \end{cases} \]

question.text: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,2,4)$ lies on $C$, and that $f_y = \dfrac{3x+y}{\sqrt{6xy+y^2}}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.explanation:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z = f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,2,4)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial y} \Bigg|_{(1,2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial y}$ at $(1,2)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_y\left(1,2\right) &= \dfrac{3(1)+(2)}{\sqrt{6(1)(2)+(2)^2}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5}{\sqrt{16}}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac 54 \end{align*}

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

\begin{align*} z - z|_{(1,2)} &= \dfrac {\partial z} {\partial y}\Bigg |_{(1,2)}(y-2) \\[5pt] z - 4 &= \dfrac54(y-2) \\[5pt] z &= \dfrac54y +\dfrac32 \end{align*}

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,2,4)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x = 1 \\[3pt] z = \dfrac54y +\dfrac32 \end{cases} \]

question.text: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=0.5.$ Given that the point $P(0.5,2,4)$ lies on $C$, and that $f_y = y + 2y\ln(xy) + \dfrac 1x$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.explanation:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z = f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=0.5.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(0.5,2,4)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial y} \Bigg|_{(0.5,2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial y}$ at $(0.5,2)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial z} {\partial y}\Bigg |_{(0.5,2)} &=2 + 2(2)\ln((0.5)(2)) + \dfrac 1{0.5} \\[3pt] &= 2 + 4\ln 1 + 2\\[3pt] &= 4 \end{align*}

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

\begin{align*} z - z|_{(0.5,2)} &= \dfrac {\partial z} {\partial y}\Bigg |_{(0.5,2)}(y-2) \\[5pt] z - 4 &= 4(y-2) \\[5pt] z &= 4y - 4 \end{align*}

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(0.5,2,4)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x = 0.5 \\[3pt] z = 4y - 4 \end{cases} \]

question.text: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$ Given that the point $P\left(1,\dfrac{\pi}{2},0\right)$ lies on $C$, and that $f_x = 2\sin(xy) -x\cos y$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.explanation:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z = f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P\left(1,\dfrac{\pi}{2},0\right)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial x} \Bigg|_{\left(1,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial x}$ at $\left(1,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial z} {\partial x}\Bigg |_{\left(1,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)} &= 2\sin\left(1\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)-1\cdot\cos \dfrac{\pi}{2} \\[3pt] &= 2\cdot 1 - 1\cdot 0 \\[3pt] &= 2 \end{align*}

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

\begin{align*} z - z|_{\left(1,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)} &= \dfrac {\partial z} {\partial x}\Bigg |_{\left(1,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)}\left(x-1\right) \\[5pt] z - 0 &= 2\left(x-1\right) \\[5pt] z &= 2x - 2 \end{align*}

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P\left(1,\dfrac{\pi}{2},0\right)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows: \[ \begin{cases} y = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ z = 2x-2 \end{cases} \]

question.text: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=5.$ Given that the point $P(4,5,-2)$ lies on $C$, and that $f_x = \dfrac{\sqrt{y^2-x^2}}{2x-y}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.explanation:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=5.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative $f_x(4,5).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $f_x(x,y)$ at $(4,5)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_x(4,5) &= \dfrac{\sqrt{(5)^2-(4)^2}}{2(4)-(5)} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\sqrt 9}{3} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 3 3 \\[5pt] &= 1 \end{align*}

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

\begin{align*} z - f(4,5) &= f_x(4,5)(x-4) \\[3pt] z - (-2)&= 1 (x-4) \\[3pt] z + 2 &= x-4 \\[3pt] z &= x - 6 \end{align*}

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(4,5,-2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes: \[ \begin{cases} y = 5 \\ z = x - 6 \end{cases} \]

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane $y = 5,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 0,1,0 \rangle.$

  • For the plane $z = x - 6$ (or $x-z-6=0$), a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle 1,0,-1 \rangle.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 & = \langle 0, 1, 0 \rangle \times \langle 1, 0, -1 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \begin{array}{|ccc|} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \end{array} \\[5pt] &=-\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{k} \end{align*}

Finally, since $-\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{k}$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-(-\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{k}) = \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{k}$ is also parallel to it.

question.text: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(-1,1,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that $f_x = 3e^{x+y}-\ln|xy| $, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.explanation:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative $f_x(-1,1).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $f_x(x,y)$ at $(-1,1)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_x(-1,1) &= 3e^{-1+1}-\ln|(-1)\cdot 1| \\[3pt] &= 3\cdot 1 -\ln 1 \\[3pt] &= 3-0 \\[3pt] &= 3 \end{align*}

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

\begin{align*} z - f(-1,1) &= f_x(-1,1)(x-(-1)) \\[3pt] z - (-1)&= 3 (x+1) \\[3pt] z + 1 &= 3x+3 \\[3pt] z &=3x + 2 \end{align*}

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-1,1,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes: \[ \begin{cases} y = 1 \\ z = 3x + 2 \end{cases} \]

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane $y = 1,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 0,1,0 \rangle.$

  • For the plane $z = 3x + 2$ (or $3x-z+2=0$), a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle 3,0,-1 \rangle.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 & = \langle 0, 1, 0 \rangle \times \langle 3, 0, -1 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \begin{array}{|ccc|} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & -1 \end{array} \\[5pt] &=-\mathbf{i} - 3\,\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \langle -1,0,-3 \rangle \end{align*}

Finally, since $\langle -1,0,-3 \rangle$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-\langle -1,0,-3 \rangle = \langle 1,0,3 \rangle$ is also parallel to it.

question.text: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-2.$ Given that the point $P(-2,-6,1)$ lies on $C$, and that $f_y =\dfrac{y-x}{\sqrt{x(y+x)}}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.explanation:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=-2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative $f_y(-2,-6).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $f_y(x,y)$ at $(-2,-6)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_y(-2,-6) &= \dfrac{-6-(-2)}{\sqrt{(-2)(-6+(-2))}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{-4}{\sqrt{16}} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac 4 4 \\[5pt] &= -1 \end{align*}

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

\begin{align*} z - f(-2,-6) &= f_y(-2,-6)(y-(-6)) \\[3pt] z - 1&= -1 (y+6) \\[3pt] z - 1 &= -y-6 \\[3pt] z &=-y - 5 \end{align*}

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-2,-6,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes: \[ \begin{cases} x = -2 \\ z = -y - 5 \end{cases} \]

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane $x = -2,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 1,0,0 \rangle.$

  • For the plane $z = -y - 5$ (or $y+z+5=0$), a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle 0,1,1 \rangle.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 & = \langle 1, 0, 0 \rangle \times \langle 0, 1, 1 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \begin{array}{|ccc|} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{array} \\[5pt] &=-\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \langle 0,-1,1\rangle \end{align*}

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $\langle 0,-1,1\rangle.$

question.text: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,-1,2)$ lies on $C$, and that $f_y =x^{2} \left(2 x y - 1\right)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.explanation:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative $f_y(1,-1).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $f_y(x,y)$ at $(1,-1)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_y(1,-1) &= (1)^{2} \left(2 (1) (-1) - 1\right)= -3 \end{align*}

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

\begin{align*} z - f(1,-1) &= f_y(1,-1)(y+1) \\[3pt] z - 2&= -3 (y+1) \\[3pt] z - 2 &= -3y-3 \\[3pt] z &=-3y - 1 \end{align*}

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,-1,2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes: \[ \begin{cases} x = 1 \\ z = -3y - 1 \end{cases} \]

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane $x = 1,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 1,0,0 \rangle.$

  • For the plane $z = -3y - 1$ (or $-3y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle 0,-3,-1 \rangle.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 & = \langle 1, 0, 0 \rangle \times \langle 0, -3, -1 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \begin{array}{|ccc|} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & -1 \end{array} \\[5pt] &=\mathbf{j} - 3\,\mathbf{k} \end{align*}

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $\mathbf{j} - 3\,\mathbf{k}.$

question.text: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=0.$ Given that the point $P\left(\dfrac{1}{2},0,1\right)$ lies on $C$, and that $f_x = (y+1)\cos(\pi x) + 2x\cos(\pi y)\sin(\pi x)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.explanation:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=0.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative $f_x\left(\dfrac{1}{2},0\right).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $f_x(x,y)$ at $\left(\dfrac{1}{2},0\right)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_x\left(\dfrac{1}{2},0\right) &= (0+1)\cos\left(\pi \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\right) + 2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\cos\left(\pi \cdot 0 \right) \sin\left(\pi \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\[5pt] &=\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) + \cos\left(0\right)\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \\[5pt] &= 0+1 \\[5pt] &=1 \end{align*}

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

\begin{align*} z - f\left(\dfrac{1}{2},0\right) &= f_x\left(\dfrac{1}{2},0\right)\left(x-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\[5pt] z - 1 &= 1\left(x-\dfrac 1 2\right) \\[5pt] z -1 &= x - \dfrac{1}{2} \\[5pt] z &= x+\dfrac{1}{2} \end{align*}

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P\left(\dfrac{1}{2},0,1\right)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes: \[ \begin{cases} y = 0 \\ z = x + \dfrac{1}{2} \end{cases} \]

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane $y = 0,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 0,1,0 \rangle.$

  • For the plane $z = x + \dfrac{1}{2}$ (or $x-z+\dfrac{1}{2}=0$), a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle 1,0,-1 \rangle.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 & = \langle 0, 1, 0 \rangle \times \langle 1, 0, -1 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \begin{array}{|ccc|} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \end{array} \\[5pt] &=-\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{k} \end{align*}

Finally, since $-\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{k}$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-(-\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{k}) = \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{k}$ is also parallel to it.
